case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates an implied private federal cause of action allowing private plaintiffs to seek rescission of contracts alleged to violate the Act.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Investment Company Act of 1940, Section 47(b), 15 U.S.C. § 80a-46(b) (particularly § 80a-46(b)(2) concerning the enforceability/rescission of illegal contracts).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (supported by multiple amici and the United States) argue that Section 47(b) does not itself create a private right of action. In their view, the provision supplies a remedy (unenforceability/rescission) only when a plaintiff is already in court under an expressly authorized cause of action; it does not authorize private parties to sue in federal court in the first place. They emphasize the Supreme Court’s restrictive implied-rights doctrine (focusing on statutory text and structure) and contend that reading Section 47(b) to authorize private rescission suits would improperly expand private enforcement of the ICA beyond what Congress provided, potentially inviting significant litigation and regulatory disruption.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that the plain text of Section 47(b)(2) contemplates that parties to an illegal contract may seek rescission, and that this necessarily presupposes a mechanism for private plaintiffs to bring such claims in court. They rely on the statutory language as 'rights-creating' (or at least as affirmatively authorizing contract-voiding suits) and maintain that recognizing a limited private rescission remedy is consistent with the statutory design and with the Court’s recognition, in analogous contexts, of limited contract-voiding remedies. They also downplay policy concerns by stressing the narrowness of the remedy (rescission rather than compensatory damages) and argue that private rescission claims arise infrequently and are cabined by traditional equitable principles.
key_precedents: Northwest Airlines, Inc. v. Transport Workers Union of America, 451 U.S. 77 (1981)
Touche Ross & Co. v. Redington, 442 U.S. 560 (1979)
Transamerica Mortgage Advisors, Inc. v. Lewis (TAMA), 444 U.S. 11 (1979)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s point about the phrase “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” is the best textual hook for an affirmative suit, but under Sandoval and Touche Ross that sort of remedial, court-directed language still does not supply the antecedent, rights-creating authorization to sue; it can operate once the parties are properly in court on some independent claim. Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh reinforce the structural inference: Congress expressly created targeted private actions in the ICA (notably §36(b)) and otherwise vested primary enforcement in the SEC, making it implausible that §47(b) silently adds a freestanding federal cause of action. Transamerica (TAMA) does not unsettle that conclusion because it construed different statutory text and predates our modern implied-rights methodology; at most it supports allowing rescission as a remedy ancillary to an existing cause of action, not a standalone federal claim. A narrow holding denying an implied standalone cause of action while preserving §47(b)’s availability as a rule of decision/remedy best fits our precedents and minimizes disruption to the statutory scheme.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on §47(b)(2)’s phrase “at the instance of any party” is the strongest counterpoint, but under Sandoval a remedial directive to courts does not itself create a congressionally authorized cause of action; it can just as naturally operate once parties are already before a court on some proper claim or defense. Transamerica (TAMA) does not move me because it addressed different statutory text and, in any event, predates and cannot override our modern insistence on clear, rights-creating language; as Justice Kagan notes, the ICA’s express, limited private remedy in §36(b) and the SEC-centered enforcement scheme cut strongly against implying an additional private suit from §47(b). The original public meaning of §47(b) speaks to unenforceability/rescission consequences for illegal contracts, not to who may hale whom into federal court. Accordingly, I would not infer a freestanding private right of action absent explicit congressional authorization.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point remains the phrase “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party,” which she says presupposes an affirmative suit; but under Sandoval and Touche Ross, that sort of remedial directive still does not supply the antecedent, plaintiff-authorizing cause of action. As Chief Justice Roberts explains, §47(b) can operate as a rule of decision once litigation is properly before a court—e.g., as a defense to enforcement or as a remedy ancillary to an express ICA claim—without silently creating a new federal claim. Transamerica does not compel a different result because it involved distinct statutory text and predates our modern insistence on clear congressional creation of private causes of action; the ICA’s structure, including §36(b)’s carefully cabined express private action, reinforces the inference against implying another. The practical investor-protection concerns Sotomayor raises are real, but they cannot substitute for the clear textual authorization our cases now require before we expand private enforcement beyond what Congress expressly provided.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s Sandoval/Touche Ross point seriously: remedial language alone often does not create a cause of action, and §47(b) can operate as a rule of decision once parties are properly before a court. But §47(b)(2)’s command that a court “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” is unusual in that it presupposes an affirmative invocation by a contracting party and then tightly cabins when rescission may be withheld—features that look less like a mere background remedy and more like a limited, congressionally specified enforcement mechanism. Justice Kagan and Justice Thomas’s negative-implication argument from the ICA’s express private rights (e.g., §36(b)) has weight, yet it does not overcome text that, as in Transamerica’s contract-voiding context, fairly implies a narrow rescission action rather than open-ended private enforcement. Given the investor-protection design and the practical reality that a defense-only reading often leaves dispersed investors without a meaningful path to unwind illegal contracts absent SEC action, I would adhere to recognizing only a constrained rescission claim consistent with §47(b)’s equitable guardrails.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s textual point about “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” is the best case for an affirmative suit, because it sounds like Congress anticipated a party coming into court and asking for rescission. But under Sandoval/Touche Ross (as the Chief Justice stresses), language that prescribes what a court must do once rescission is properly sought still does not answer the antecedent question—who is authorized to invoke federal jurisdiction on what cause of action—especially where the ICA elsewhere uses explicit, rights-creating terms to confer narrowly tailored private suits (e.g., §36(b)). Transamerica does not genuinely undermine that conclusion: it construed different text in a different statute and, even on its own terms, exemplifies restraint by implying only a limited remedy while rejecting broader private enforcement, which cuts against expanding §47(b) into a freestanding federal claim. The more coherent, workable reading is that §47(b) supplies a contract-unenforceability/rescission consequence available as a defense or as ancillary relief when some independently authorized claim places the parties in court.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press the textual force of “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party,” which sounds like an affirmative request for relief. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, under Sandoval and Touche Ross that sort of remedial, court-directed language does not itself supply the antecedent, rights-creating authorization to sue; it can operate as a rule of decision once a party is properly in court through some other valid cause of action. Transamerica does not change that result because it construed different statutory text in a different statute and predates our modern implied-right framework; and the ICA’s carefully cabined express private remedies (notably §36(b)) reinforce the structural inference against silently creating a new federal cause of action. On an originalist/textualist view, §47(b) speaks to the legal consequences for unlawful contracts (unenforceability/rescission), not who may hale whom into federal court.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point remains the “at the instance of any party” phrasing in §47(b)(2), which sounds like it anticipates an affirmative request for rescission and she analogizes to Transamerica. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas explain, under Sandoval and Touche Ross remedial language—even language that presupposes a court proceeding—does not itself supply the antecedent, plaintiff-authorizing cause of action; it can function as a rule of decision once the parties are properly before a court on some other claim or defense. Transamerica does not compel a different result here because it involved different statutory text and predates (and sits uneasily with) our modern implied-rights framework, and the ICA’s structure—especially the targeted express private action in §36(b) and SEC-centered enforcement—makes it implausible that Congress silently created a freestanding federal rescission suit in §47(b). On an institutionalist view, a narrow holding that §47(b) supplies a remedy but not a standalone federal cause of action best respects text, structure, and our implied-rights precedents without overextending private enforcement beyond what Congress clearly authorized.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on §47(b)(2)’s “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” is the best textual hook for an affirmative suit, but under Sandoval and Touche Ross that sort of remedial, rule-of-decision phrasing does not supply the antecedent, rights-creating authorization to sue in federal court. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, the ICA’s structure—expressly providing limited private actions like §36(b) while otherwise vesting primary enforcement in the SEC—makes it implausible that Congress silently created a freestanding private rescission claim in §47(b). Transamerica does not materially change the analysis because it construed different statutory text in a different statute and predates our stricter implied-rights framework; at most, §47(b) governs the availability of rescission once a party is properly before a court on some other valid cause of action. I therefore remain persuaded that §47(b) can do work as a remedy/defense without creating a standalone federal cause of action.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “at the instance of any party” point is the toughest textual hook because it sounds like Congress anticipated a party affirmatively asking a court for rescission, and Transamerica lends some historical support for a narrow rescission implication. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Sandoval and Touche Ross require more than remedial directives that assume litigation; they demand rights-creating, plaintiff-authorizing language, and §47(b) reads more naturally as a rule of decision governing the effect of illegality once a court is properly seized of a case through some other cause of action. The ICA’s overall structure—expressly creating a targeted private right in §36(b) while otherwise relying on SEC enforcement—makes it especially hard for me, as a matter of institutional restraint, to infer an additional freestanding federal cause of action from §47(b)’s remedial phrasing. On practical consequences, I share Sotomayor’s concern about investor access to relief, but under modern implied-rights doctrine that policy gap is for Congress to close; §47(b) can still do meaningful work as a remedy/defense in existing suits without silently expanding federal jurisdiction.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under our implied-rights cases, the question is whether Congress created a private cause of action in the statute’s text and structure, not whether such a remedy would be sensible. See Alexander v. Sandoval and Touche Ross & Co. v. Redington. Section 47(b)(2) speaks in remedial terms—how a “court may not deny rescission” once the issue is properly before it—but it does not contain rights-creating language authorizing private plaintiffs to sue in the first instance, and it can operate as a rule of decision or defense in contract litigation without implying a new federal claim. Moreover, unlike the statute in Transamerica Mortgage Advisors, Inc. v. Lewis, the ICA contains express private rights of action elsewhere, which strongly counsels against inferring an additional, freestanding rescission action from §47(b).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 47(b) speaks to the enforceability and rescission of contracts that “violate” the Act, but it does not contain rights-creating language or an express authorization for private plaintiffs to sue in federal court; under the Court’s modern textual approach, that omission is dispositive. Alexander v. Sandoval instructs that private rights of action must be created by Congress, and courts may not infer them from statutory purpose or remedial desirability. The ICA’s structure reinforces this reading because Congress provided limited express private enforcement elsewhere (e.g., § 36(b)), while generally assigning enforcement to the SEC—confirming that § 47(b) supplies, at most, a rule of decision or remedy once a proper cause of action exists, not a freestanding private cause of action. Touche Ross and Northwest Airlines likewise caution against implying private causes of action absent clear textual and structural evidence of congressional intent.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 47(b) is framed as a remedial and enforceability provision (“a contract … is unenforceable” and a court “may not deny rescission” in certain circumstances), not as rights-creating language authorizing private plaintiffs to file suit in federal court. Under this Court’s modern implied-rights doctrine, we do not infer a private cause of action absent clear textual evidence in the statute’s structure and language, and Sandoval and Touche Ross instruct that a remedy does not itself create a right to sue. Transamerica Mortgage Advisors (TAMA) does not compel a different result because it read different statutory text (§ 215 of the IAA) and, in any event, recognized only a narrow contract-voiding implication rather than a general private enforcement mechanism; here, reading § 47(b) as an affirmative cause of action would expand private enforcement of the ICA beyond what Congress expressly provided. The practical consequences of inviting broad private rescission litigation in a heavily regulated field further counsel against implying a cause of action where Congress did not clearly create one.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 47(b)(2) does more than supply a remedy once a plaintiff is already properly in court; by directing that an illegal ICA contract is unenforceable and that a court "may not deny rescission at the instance of any party" unless equitable conditions are met, it presupposes that a contracting party may affirmatively invoke the courts to obtain that rescission. This Court in Transamerica Mortgage Advisors, Inc. v. Lewis recognized that materially similar “void” language in the IAA fairly implies a specific, limited private action for rescission, even while rejecting broader damages remedies; that middle-course approach respects Sandoval’s focus on text and structure without inventing expansive private enforcement. Reading §47(b) to allow only a defense (or only SEC-invoked litigation) would undercut Congress’s investor-protection design by leaving vulnerable shareholders bound to prohibited contracts unless the Government happens to sue. The remedy is also self-limiting—rescission governed by equitable principles—mitigating the petitioners’ floodgates concerns while ensuring practical access to justice for those harmed by unlawful fund arrangements.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 47(b) is framed as a contracts/remedies provision—making certain unlawful contracts unenforceable and describing rescission consequences—but it does not itself speak in rights-creating terms or authorize any person to sue, which under Sandoval is the central textual inquiry for implied causes of action. The ICA’s structure reinforces that reading because Congress provided express, carefully limited private enforcement elsewhere (e.g., §§ 36(b) and 30(h)), and under Touche Ross and Northwest Airlines we do not infer additional private causes of action from remedial language alone. Transamerica (TAMA) is distinguishable: there the Court found a limited rescission action because the IAA provision’s text “fairly implies” such a suit, but even there the Court rejected a broader damages remedy—confirming the Court’s modern restraint and the need for clearer authorization than §47(b) provides. Reading §47(b) as a freestanding private cause of action would also create a mismatched enforcement scheme relative to the SEC’s central role and the statute’s calibrated express remedies.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 47(b) supplies a remedial consequence (unenforceability/rescission of an illegal contract) but its text does not create a freestanding private right to sue; under our implied-rights cases, “rights-creating” language and clear congressional authorization are required. Alexander v. Sandoval and Touche Ross instruct that courts may not infer a private cause of action from remedial or enforcement-adjacent provisions absent textual direction, and the ICA’s structure—containing express private causes of action elsewhere—strongly suggests Congress did not mean to add another by implication. Section 47(b)(2)’s instruction that a court “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” can operate as a rule governing rescission once parties are properly before a court (including as a defense), without opening federal courthouses to new private suits. Transamerica Mortgage Advisors (TAMA) is distinguishable because it relied on materially different contract-voiding language and does not override Sandoval’s demand for clear textual authorization, especially where Congress has elsewhere spoken expressly.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under this Court’s implied-rights doctrine, the question is whether Congress clearly created a private cause of action in the statute’s text and structure, not whether a private remedy would be useful. Section 47(b)(2) of the ICA, 15 U.S.C. § 80a-46(b)(2), functions as a rule about the enforceability/rescission of unlawful contracts, but it does not contain the kind of rights-creating, plaintiff-authorizing language that Sandoval and Touche Ross require to recognize a freestanding private suit. The ICA’s structure underscores that conclusion because Congress expressly created limited private enforcement elsewhere (e.g., § 36(b)), while largely assigning enforcement to the SEC—making it implausible that § 47(b) silently adds a broad new private rescission action. Transamerica Mortgage Advisors is distinguishable because it inferred a limited rescission action from materially different statutory language, and here the better reading is that § 47(b) supplies a remedy only when a plaintiff is already properly in court under an express cause of action or a valid state-law claim.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under this Court’s implied-rights doctrine, the question is whether Congress “display[ed] an intent” in the statutory text and structure to create a private cause of action, not whether a private remedy would be sensible policy. See Alexander v. Sandoval, 532 U.S. 275 (2001); Touche Ross & Co. v. Redington, 442 U.S. 560 (1979). Section 47(b)(2) of the ICA, 15 U.S.C. § 80a-46(b)(2), speaks in remedial/enforceability terms (providing that an illegal contract is unenforceable and may be rescinded), but it does not contain the sort of rights-creating language that would authorize private plaintiffs to sue in the first place. Transamerica Mortgage Advisors, Inc. v. Lewis recognized a limited rescission remedy under the IAA’s parallel provision based on that statute’s particular text, but Sandoval and Northwest Airlines counsel against extending that reasoning to infer a freestanding private cause of action here absent a clear textual hook in the ICA.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under this Court’s implied-rights framework, the question is whether Congress clearly created a private cause of action in the statutory text and structure, not whether a private remedy would be useful. See Alexander v. Sandoval, 532 U.S. 275 (2001), and Touche Ross & Co. v. Redington, 442 U.S. 560 (1979). Section 47(b)(2) of the ICA, 15 U.S.C. § 80a-46(b)(2), speaks in remedial terms about the unenforceability and rescission of unlawful contracts but does not contain the rights-creating, plaintiff-focused language or jurisdictional authorization that typically signals an affirmative private suit, especially given the ICA’s express enforcement scheme elsewhere. Although Transamerica Mortgage Advisors, Inc. v. Lewis, 444 U.S. 11 (1979), recognized a limited rescission remedy under the IAA’s contract-voiding provision, Sandoval counsels caution against extending implied causes of action beyond what Congress affirmatively provided, and I would read § 47(b) as supplying a remedy only when a plaintiff is properly before the court under an existing cause of action.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates an implied private federal cause of action allowing private plaintiffs to sue for rescission of contracts alleged to violate the Act.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Investment Company Act of 1940, Section 47(b), 15 U.S.C. § 80a-46(b) (particularly § 80a-46(b)(2)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (supported by several amici and the United States) argue that Section 47(b) does not itself create a private right of action; it is a remedial/contract-effect provision that may describe the consequence of illegality (e.g., voidability) but does not contain the rights-creating text and structural signals that Sandoval and related cases require to imply a private cause of action. They contend that recognizing such a claim would improperly expand private enforcement under the ICA beyond what Congress specified, potentially inviting broad, opportunistic litigation against registered funds and regulated entities, and would circumvent the ICA’s carefully reticulated enforcement scheme (including SEC enforcement and the Act’s express private remedies in other provisions).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that the plain text of Section 47(b)(2) contemplates rescission as a remedy and, consistent with that text, parties to contracts that violate the ICA may seek rescission in court. They maintain that the statute’s language and structure supply the requisite affirmative evidence of congressional intent to allow at least this limited private remedy (rescission/voiding of illegal contracts, not compensatory damages), and that recognizing such a narrow cause of action aligns with historical treatment of illegal contracts in federal securities statutes and does not open the door to broader damages remedies.
key_precedents: Northwest Airlines, Inc. v. Transport Workers Union of America, 451 U.S. 77 (1981)
Touche Ross & Co. v. Redington, 442 U.S. 560 (1979)
Transamerica Mortgage Advisors, Inc. v. Lewis (TAMA), 444 U.S. 11 (1979)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press that §47(b)(2)’s “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” sounds like an affirmative remedial directive, and Transamerica shows that “void”/rescission language can sometimes support a limited remedy. But under Sandoval and Touche Ross, that sort of remedial instruction still does not supply the necessary rights-creating text or structural evidence of a freestanding private cause of action, and—as Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize—the ICA’s reticulated scheme with an express private right in §36(b) counsels against implying another. The more coherent, minimal reading is that §47(b) sets the rule of decision and limits equitable discretion once rescission is properly before a court on some independent cause of action, which preserves Transamerica’s narrowness without extending it beyond its distinct statutory context. That narrow holding best protects institutional legitimacy by respecting Congress’s enforcement design and our modern implied-rights precedents.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best textual point is that §47(b)(2) says a court may not deny rescission “at the instance of any party,” which she reads as presupposing a privately invocable rescission action. But under Sandoval (as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize), remedial or court-directed language is not rights-creating language; §47(b) is more naturally a rule of decision about the consequences of illegality and a constraint on equitable discretion once rescission is otherwise properly before a court. Transamerica does not overcome that inference because it relied on materially different “void” language and predates Sandoval’s stricter methodology; importing it here would conflict with the ICA’s reticulated structure with express private remedies elsewhere and SEC-centered enforcement. On an original public-meaning textualist reading, §47(b) can supply a remedy/defense without creating a freestanding federal cause of action.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point remains the phrase in §47(b)(2) that a court “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party,” which she reads as an affirmative entitlement to sue; but under Sandoval that remedial command still lacks rights-creating language and is naturally read, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, as a rule of decision constraining equitable discretion once rescission is properly before a court on some independent cause of action. Transamerica does not undermine that conclusion because its inference turned on materially different “void” language and an older methodology, and even there the Court refused to imply broader remedies—making it a weak foundation for creating a freestanding federal claim here. Structurally, the ICA’s reticulated, SEC-centered enforcement scheme and Congress’s express creation of private rights elsewhere (e.g., §36(b)) reinforce the view that §47(b) addresses consequences/remedies, not who may sue. Given the practical consequences of expanding private enforcement beyond what the text clearly authorizes, I remain with Petitioner.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The strongest opposing point, pressed by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan, is that §47(b) is merely a rule of decision about contract consequences once a separate cause of action is properly in court; but that reading struggles to give meaningful work to §47(b)(2)’s specific directive that a court “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” absent enumerated equitable conditions. Under Sandoval, we should not create broad implied enforcement regimes, yet §47(b)(2) is not free-floating remedial verbiage—it is a targeted remedial command keyed to “any party,” which is difficult to operationalize if no party can ever invoke it affirmatively, and thus functions much like the limited rescission inference in Transamerica even if the ICA’s structure is more reticulated. Justice Thomas’s structural argument about express private remedies elsewhere is serious, but it does not negate Congress’s choice to speak in unusually mandatory, party-invoking terms here; I would read §47(b) to imply only a narrow rescission/unwinding remedy (not damages) to protect investors and avoid leaving enforcement solely to discretionary SEC action. The Petitioner’s approach risks making §47(b)(2) largely inert in the very circumstances—unlawful fund contracts—where vulnerable investors most need a judicially enforceable unwind.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that §47(b)(2)’s “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” sounds like Congress expected litigants to ask for rescission, but under Sandoval that expectation does not itself supply the missing cause-of-action hook; it is equally coherent as a remedial rule of decision once a rescission request is properly before a court on some independent claim. Chief Justice Roberts’s structural point strengthens that reading: the ICA is a reticulated scheme with express private remedies (notably §36(b)) and SEC-centered enforcement, so treating §47(b) as a freestanding implied action would be a comparatively large, textually unsupported step that would distort statutory coherence. Transamerica (TAMA), which Justice Sotomayor invokes, is meaningfully distinguishable because it rested on different “void” language and a pre-Sandoval methodology; here, §47(b)’s “may” formulation reads more like a constraint on equitable discretion than an affirmative rights-creating grant. On pragmatic textualist terms, the narrower construction is more workable: it gives §47(b)(2) operative force without opening a new federal cause of action that Congress did not clearly authorize.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s point about §47(b)(2) (“may not deny rescission at the instance of any party”) has intuitive force, but under Sandoval the inquiry is whether Congress clearly created a private cause of action, not whether it specified a desirable remedy once litigation is properly underway. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, the phrase is more naturally read as a limit on equitable discretion—a rule of decision about the consequences of illegality—rather than rights-creating language authorizing any party to file a freestanding federal suit. Transamerica does not genuinely undermine that reading because it turned on different statutory text (“void”) and predates Sandoval’s insistence on clearer textual signals, and importing its inference here would clash with the ICA’s reticulated scheme and Congress’s choice to provide express private actions elsewhere. On a textualist/originalist account faithful to separation of powers, §47(b) can supply rescission when some independent claim is before a court, but it does not itself confer the right to sue.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point remains that §47(b)(2) says a court “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party,” which sounds like an affirmative entitlement and is awkward if no one can ever invoke it. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, Sandoval requires clear rights-creating authorization to sue; a remedial command to courts can operate as a rule of decision once a case is properly before the court, without itself creating a freestanding federal cause of action. Transamerica (TAMA) does not undermine that conclusion because it turned on different “void” language and predates Sandoval’s more text-and-structure-focused approach, and reading §47(b) to create a new implied cause would sit uneasily with the ICA’s reticulated, SEC-centered scheme and Congress’s express private remedy choices elsewhere. Institutionally and practically, the narrower reading—§47(b) supplies rescission only when some independent cause of action brings the parties into court—best respects precedent and avoids expanding private enforcement beyond what Congress clearly enacted.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point remains the textual force of §47(b)(2)’s directive that a court “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party,” which plausibly sounds like an affirmative entitlement. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, Sandoval and Touche Ross require more than remedial or court-directed language; the statute must create a right and a cause of action, and §47(b) reads more naturally as a rule of decision governing the consequences of illegality once the parties are properly before a court on some independent claim. Transamerica does not materially alter that analysis because its inference turned on different “void” language and a pre-Sandoval approach, and importing it here would sit uneasily with the ICA’s reticulated scheme, including Congress’s express creation of a private action in §36(b). On a textualist/originalist view attentive to structure and precedent, §47(b) supplies a rescission remedy when available, not a freestanding authorization for private plaintiffs to sue.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s point about §47(b)(2)’s “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” is the strongest textual hook for an implied remedy, because it sounds like an entitlement that anticipates a litigant asking a court for rescission. But under Sandoval’s approach—and as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize—remedial, court-directed language is not the same thing as rights-creating language authorizing a freestanding federal cause of action; it can function as a constraint on equitable discretion once rescission is properly before the court on some independent claim. Transamerica is not enough to overcome that because it turned on materially different “void” language and predates the Court’s insistence on clearer textual signals before implying private enforcement, and importing it here would sit uneasily with the ICA’s reticulated scheme that includes express private remedies elsewhere. Considering consequences and procedural fairness, I remain persuaded §47(b) can operate defensively or as a rule of decision without inviting an implied, affirmative federal rescission action in every illegality dispute.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Alexander v. Sandoval, we do not imply private causes of action absent clear rights-creating text and structural evidence that Congress meant private plaintiffs to enforce the statute. Section 47(b) functions as a remedial/contract-effect provision—specifying when contracts are unenforceable and when a court may not deny rescission—but it does not itself identify a protected class or create a substantive entitlement enforceable in a private suit, especially given the ICA’s overall enforcement design and its express private remedies elsewhere. Transamerica Mortgage Advisors v. Lewis is distinguishable because the Court found a limited rescission remedy tied to the IAA’s particular “void” language; here, reading §80a-46(b)(2) as an affirmative authorization to sue would expand private enforcement beyond what the ICA’s text and structure clearly provide. A narrow holding that §47(b) supplies a remedy only when an independent cause of action exists best respects precedent and preserves institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under a strict textualist approach, §47(b) speaks to the legal effect of contracts made or performed in violation of the Act and the availability of rescission as a remedy, but it does not contain the rights-creating language that Alexander v. Sandoval requires to infer a private federal cause of action. The Act’s structure reinforces that conclusion: when Congress intended private enforcement it did so expressly (e.g., ICA §36(b)), while otherwise committing enforcement to the SEC, which counsels against implying additional private suits. Transamerica Mortgage Advisors, Inc. v. Lewis is distinguishable because the IAA provision at issue there was read to “fairly imply” only a limited rescission remedy from its particular text and context; §47(b) here is better understood as a rule of decision/contract-consequence provision that can operate defensively or in appropriate equitable postures without creating a new freestanding private right. Consistent with Touche Ross and Northwest Airlines, courts should not create private causes of action absent affirmative evidence in the statute’s text and structure.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 47(b) is framed as a contract-effect/remedial provision—stating when a contract is unenforceable or subject to rescission—but it does not contain the sort of rights-creating language that Alexander v. Sandoval requires to infer a private cause of action. Read in the ICA’s broader structure, Congress provided specific enforcement mechanisms (notably SEC enforcement and express private remedies elsewhere), which counsels against implying an additional private suit that could expand litigation beyond what Congress authorized. Transamerica Mortgage Advisors (TAMA) is distinguishable: there the Court found a limited rescission remedy based on the particular statutory language of IAA §215, but it refused to infer broader remedies, and Sandoval’s subsequent emphasis on clear textual indicia of congressional intent makes importing TAMA’s implication into ICA §47(b) especially unwarranted. Given the statute’s text and the practical consequences of opening a new avenue of private enforcement against regulated funds, I would not recognize an implied private right of action under §47(b).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 47(b)(2)’s directive that “a court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” unless specified equitable conditions are met is remedial language that presupposes judicial enforcement and, for parties to an unlawful contract, meaningfully implies access to a federal forum for rescission. As in Transamerica Mortgage Advisors, Inc. v. Lewis (TAMA), where § 215(b) was held to “fairly impl[y] a right to specific and limited” relief (rescission) even absent an express cause of action for damages, § 47(b) can be read to authorize a similarly narrow private remedy limited to undoing illegal contracts rather than expanding into broad damages litigation. This reading also advances the ICA’s investor-protection purpose by ensuring that vulnerable investors are not left solely to discretionary agency enforcement when the statute itself specifies a rescission standard. While Sandoval cautions against freewheeling implication, the text here contains the kind of focused remedial command that supplies affirmative evidence of congressional intent for at least this limited form of private enforcement.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 47(b) is framed as a remedial consequence provision—addressing the enforceability of unlawful contracts—rather than as rights-creating language authorizing “any person” to sue, which Sandoval and its predecessors (e.g., Touche Ross; Northwest Airlines) require as affirmative evidence of congressional intent to create a private cause of action. Unlike the IAA provision in Transamerica Mortgage Advisors (TAMA), § 47(b)(2)’s focus on what a court “may” do and its integration into the ICA’s broader, SEC-centered enforcement scheme counsels against inferring a new private federal action that Congress did not expressly provide. Reading § 47(b) to supply rescission only when a plaintiff is already properly in court under some other cause of action preserves statutory coherence and workability while respecting the ICA’s “carefully reticulated” remedial structure. In short, § 47(b) can describe a remedy (or a defense) without itself creating the standalone federal right to sue that respondents seek.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 47(b) speaks in remedial/contract-consequence terms and lacks the sort of rights-creating language that this Court has demanded before recognizing implied private causes of action. Under Alexander v. Sandoval, the question is congressional intent as expressed in the statute’s text and structure, and the ICA’s reticulated enforcement scheme—including express private remedies elsewhere—counsels against implying another. Section 47(b)(2)’s direction that “a court may not deny rescission” in certain circumstances presupposes a court’s power when an appropriate cause of action exists, but it does not itself create one, much as Touche Ross and Northwest Airlines refused to infer rights from provisions that did not themselves confer them. Transamerica (TAMA) is distinguishable because it inferred a limited rescission remedy from the IAA’s §215 in its particular statutory setting, and Sandoval’s later approach reinforces that we do not expand private enforcement absent clear textual authorization.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Sandoval and related cases, the judicial task is to identify clear congressional intent in the statutory text and structure to create a private cause of action, and §47(b) reads as a remedial/contract-effect provision rather than rights-creating authorization to sue. Section 47(b)(2)’s direction that a court “may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” functions as a limitation on equitable discretion once rescission is otherwise properly before a court; it does not itself supply the affirmative, rights-creating language and enforcement architecture that Sandoval requires. Recognizing an implied rescission action here would risk expanding private enforcement beyond the ICA’s carefully reticulated scheme—especially given that Congress provided express private remedies elsewhere in the Act—counseling restraint and respect for institutional legitimacy. TAMA is distinguishable because it relied on particular “void” language in IAA §215 that this Court held “fairly implies” only a limited remedy there, and that inference does not override Sandoval’s demand for clear textual signals in the ICA’s different structure and wording.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 47(b) speaks in remedial terms about the effect of illegality on contracts and when a court may deny rescission, but it does not contain the kind of rights-creating language that Alexander v. Sandoval and Touche Ross require before recognizing an implied private cause of action. Read in context, §47(b)(2) presupposes the existence of a proper plaintiff and forum but does not itself supply the affirmative evidence of congressional intent to authorize private enforcement, especially given the ICA’s detailed enforcement scheme and its express private remedies elsewhere. Transamerica Mortgage Advisors recognized a limited rescission action under the IAA’s §215 based on that provision’s “void” language and structure, but that reasoning does not overcome Sandoval’s later insistence on clear statutory authorization, and §47(b) is better understood as a rule of decision for courts when rescission is otherwise properly sought. Methodological consistency counsels against implying a new federal cause of action from text that regulates remedies without expressly granting a private right to sue.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Alexander v. Sandoval and Touche Ross, the key question is whether Congress provided rights-creating language and structural signals of a private cause of action; Section 47(b) reads as a remedial/contract-effect rule governing when a court may grant rescission, not as an affirmative authorization for private plaintiffs to sue. Section 47(b)(2)’s directive that a court may not deny rescission “at the instance of any party” can operate as a defense or remedial constraint once a party is properly before a court, without creating a freestanding federal claim, and the ICA’s express private remedies elsewhere reinforce that Congress knew how to create such causes of action when it chose. Transamerica Mortgage Advisors (TAMA) does not compel the opposite result because it relied on materially different “void” language in the IAA and, even there, the Court refused to infer broader implied rights absent clear textual grounding. Given the practical consequences of expanding private enforcement beyond the Act’s reticulated scheme, I would not imply a new federal cause of action from Section 47(b).
